questions.q: Of the three security layers — authentication, authorization, encryption — which one does this lesson say governance architecture actually lives in?
options: Authentication
Authorization
None of the three — governance is a separate fourth layer
Encryption
questions.explain: Authentication and encryption are layers governance assumes already exist; authorization — deciding what an identity can do — is where governance architecture itself lives.

questions.q: In the governance-specific version of defense in depth, what does a masking policy provide that an access policy alone does not?
options: A replacement for classification entirely
A second, independent line of defense that doesn't depend on the access policy being configured correctly
A faster query response time
Automatic encryption of the underlying storage
questions.explain: The lesson's defense-in-depth point is that masking, attached to the same tag, protects data even if the access policy itself is misconfigured.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue the metadata/catalog layer itself needs strong security, not just the data it describes?
options: Catalogs are never covered by any security policy in practice
Metadata is inherently more valuable than the data it describes
If the catalog is readable by everyone, an attacker can learn where sensitive data lives and how it's protected without touching the data itself
The catalog always contains a full copy of the production data
questions.explain: Reading an open catalog can hand an attacker a map of exactly where valuable data lives and how it's defended — often a faster path to a breach than attacking the data directly.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what does governance's role look like in the encryption layer specifically?
options: Writing the actual cryptographic algorithms used to encrypt data at rest
Governance has no relationship to encryption at all
Replacing encryption entirely with access policies
Making sure the right data is classified and routed to the right encryption and handling requirements, not implementing the encryption algorithm itself
questions.explain: The lesson treats encryption as a baseline governance assumes, while governance's own job is correct classification and routing, not the cryptography itself.

questions.q: What is the stated path this chapter takes, starting from this lesson?
options: A single lesson covering everything, with no further chapters
Broad security architecture, then access-control mechanisms, then policy as code, then real platforms, then automation
Straight from this lesson to governance strategy, skipping platforms entirely
Automation first, then working backward to broad architecture concepts
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lays out Lessons 18 through 21 as moving from broad security architecture down to specific mechanisms, code, platforms, and automation.
